sudan.summary: تواجه التعديلات الأخيرة في القانون الجنائي السوداني انتقادات واسعة، حيث حذرت مجموعة محامو الطوارئ من تعديل المادة 51 الذي يوسع نطاق التجريم ليشمل النشر في الوسائط الإعلامية والإلكترونية. يُعتبر هذا التعديل تهديدًا لحرية الصحافة والتعبير، حيث يمكن أن يُستخدم لملاحقة الصحافيين والنشطاء بسبب ما ينشرونه. وقد أبدت نقابة الصحافيين السودانيين قلقها من أن هذه التعديلات قد تؤدي إلى رقابة ذاتية بين الصحافيين، مما يحد من قدرتهم على تناول القضايا الحساسة. من جهة أخرى، دافع وزير العدل عن التعديل، مؤكدًا أنه يهدف إلى تجريم تأييد مرتكبي الجرائم ضد الدولة، وليس التضييق على الصحافيين. ومع ذلك، يطالب العديد من الناشطين بإلغاء هذه التعديلات لضمان حرية التعبير وحماية حقوق الإنسان في السودان، مشددين على ضرورة مواءمة التشريعات مع المعايير الدولية.

Adel Abdelrheem 24 أكتوبر 2026 • تحديث : 24 أكتوبر 2026 SUDAN الخرطوم/ عادل عبد الرحيم / الأناضول أعلنت لجنة الأمل للعودة الطوعية، السبت، تسيير 25 حافلة تقل 1225 سودانيا من العاصمة المصرية القاهرة إلى السودان، ضمن برنامج العودة الطوعية. وقال رئيس اللجنة محمد وداعة، في تصريحات صحفية بالقاهرة، إن 25 حافلة تحمل على متنها 1225 من طلاب التعليم العام ومنسوبي الخدمة المدنية وأسرهم، بحسب وكالة الأنباء السودانية. ​وأضاف وداعة، أن التفويج شمل اليوم بعض مؤسسات الدولة، ومنسوبي الإذاعة والتلفزيون، والسلطة القضائية، ووزارتي الثروة الحيوانية والعدل، وديوان الحسابات، والطيران المدني. ولفت إلى أن التركيز خلال الفترة الحالية ينصب على إعادة منسوبي الخدمة المدنية، لتمكينهم من استئناف العمل في مؤسساتهم، وفق توجيهات رئيس وزراء البلاد كامل إدريس، مؤخرا. وأكد أن عودة هذه الفئات تمثل خطوة مهمة نحو تحقيق الاستقرار الأسري، بما يسهم بدوره في التنمية المجتمعية. وفي 10 أكتوبر/ تشرين الأول الجاري، أعلنت لجنة الأمل تسيير 18 حافلة تقل 882 سودانيا من القاهرة إلى السودان، ضمن برنامج العودة الطوعية. وخلال سبتمبر/ أيلول الماضي، جرى نقل 4073 سودانيا إلى بلادهم عبر 7 رحلات شملت 83 حافلة، بحسب اللجنة. ومنذ اندلاع الحرب بين الجيش السوداني وقوات الدعم السريع في أبريل/ نيسان 2023، غادر أكثر من 1.2 مليون سوداني إلى مصر، وفق تقديرات رسمية، فيما كان يقيم فيها نحو 5 ملايين سوداني قبل الحرب، لتصبح مصر إحدى أبرز وجهات الفارين من القتال. وحتى نهاية عام 2025، عاد إلى السودان طوعا نحو 428 ألفا و676 شخصا، وفق أرقام سبق أن أعلنها السفير السوداني عبد القادر عبد الله. وجاءت عمليات العودة في أعقاب مبادرة أطلقتها السلطات المصرية في أكتوبر/ تشرين الأول 2025، لنقل السودانيين الراغبين في العودة عبر قطار مخصص من القاهرة إلى أسوان. وأسفرت الحرب، وفق تقديرات أممية ودولية، عن مقتل عشرات الآلاف ونزوح نحو 13 مليون شخص. وبرنامج العودة الطوعية للسودانيين من مصر هو مبادرة مخصصة لتيسير وتفويج المواطنين السودانيين الراغبين في العودة إلى وطنهم بشكل اختياري ومجاني، وتشرف عليه آلية وطنية تُعرف باسم "لجنة الأمل للعودة الطوعية". news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription السودان يطالب «يونيسفا» بالتحقيق في الهجوم على سوق رئيسي بأبيي - سودان تربيون
sudan.content: السودان يطالب «يونيسفا» بالتحقيق في الهجوم على سوق رئيسي بأبيي - سودان تربيون تخطى الى المحتوى من نحن اتصل بنا English الأحد , 25 أكتوبر - 2026 سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية سياسة الأخبار تقصي الحقائق اقتصاد دولي اقاليم الرأي English سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية ابيي السودان يطالب «يونيسفا» بالتحقيق في الهجوم على سوق رئيسي بأبيي ابيي السودان يطالب «يونيسفا» بالتحقيق في الهجوم على سوق رئيسي بأبيي 24 أكتوبر 2026 في ابيي , الأخبار 0 أفراد من بعثة يونيسفا يخمدون الحريق الذي اندلع في سوق النعام، عقب الهجوم الذي أسفر عن مقتل 80 شخصًا. الخرطوم 24 أكتوبر 2026 – دعا رئيس اللجنة الإشرافية لمنطقة أبيي من جانب السودان الخير أبو مريدات، السبت، بعثة الأمم المتحدة الأمنية المؤقتة “يونيسفا” إلى إجراء تحقيق وتحديد الجهات المسؤولة عن الهجوم على سوق النعام. ونفذت طائرات مسيّرة في 19 أكتوبر الحالي، هجوماً على سوق النعام، المعروف أيضاً باسم ” أميت”، أسفر عن مقتل 80 شخصاً وإصابة 19 آخرين، فيما لا يزال أشخاص في عداد المفقودين، وفقاً للأمم المتحدة. وقال أبو مريدات، في تصريح صحفي، إنه “يدعو بعثة يونيسفا إلى إجراء تحقيق عاجل وشفاف لكشف ملابسات الهجوم على سوق النعام وتحديد الجهات المسؤولة عنه، بما يضمن المساءلة وعدم إفلات المتورطين من العقاب”. وأبدى أسفه إزاء الهجوم وسقوط ضحايا مدنيين، مشدداً على أن حماية أرواح المدنيين وصون أمنهم وسلامتهم تمثل أولوية ومسؤولية أساسية. وأشار إلى أن السودان جاد في الاضطلاع بمسؤولياته تجاه حماية مواطنيه والعمل على تجنيب سكان المنطقة مخاطر الحرب والهجمات المسلحة. والجمعة، نفت وزارة الخارجية السودانية صلة الجيش بالهجوم على سوق النعام، وقالت إنه يشبه القصف الذي شنته قوات الدعم السريع في ديسمبر 2025 على مقر بعثة يونيسفا في كادقلي بجنوب كردفان، والذي أودى بحياة عدد من قوات حفظ السلام. واتهمت وزارة خارجية جنوب السودان الجيش السوداني بتنفيذ الهجوم كما استدعت سفير السودان في جوبا وأبلغته احتجاجها على القصف. وطالب أبو مريدات بضرورة التعامل بحزم مع وجود الجماعات المسلحة الخارجة عن سلطات الدولة والمرتزقة المتنافسين على النفوذ داخل منطقة أبيي أو في محيطها. وأوضح أن التساهل مع هذه المظاهر المسلحة أسهم في تهيئة بيئة أمنية مضطربة تزيد من احتمالات وقوع مثل هذه الحوادث، الأمر الذي يستدعي اتخاذ تدابير جادة وفعالة لمنع تكرارها وحماية المدنيين. وتفرض قوات الدعم السريع ومليشيات متحالفة معها سيطرتها على أجزاء واسعة من سوق النعام، مع فرض ضرائب على حركة التجارة الداخلة إلى دارفور وكردفان. وتحول سوق النعام، بعد اندلاع النزاع في السودان منتصف أبريل 2023، من سوق محلية إلى مركز رئيسي لتجارة الوقود والغذاء ومواد البناء والأدوية، إضافة إلى السلع التي تتدفق من جنوب السودان إلى كردفان ودارفور. وجدد أبو مريدات تأكيد التزام السودان بتعهداته الدولية والاتفاقيات الموقعة بشأن منطقة أبيي، واحترام القرارات الدولية الرامية إلى الحفاظ على أمن المنطقة واستقرارها. وقال إن تحقيق الاستقرار في أبيي يتطلب تعاوناً مسؤولاً والتزاماً عملياً بالاتفاقيات القائمة، والعمل المشترك من أجل حماية المدنيين وصون أمن المنطقة وتجنيب سكانها تداعيات الحرب. وتتنازع الخرطوم وجوبا على السيادة على أبيي الغنية بالنفط، حيث فشل البلدان في الاتفاق على من يحق له المشاركة في استفتاء تقرير مصير المنطقة، المنصوص عليه في اتفاقية السلام الشامل لعام 2005، بسبب رفض قبيلة الدينكا نقوك مشاركة الرحل من قبيلة المسيرية في الاستفتاء. الكلمات: أبيي الامم المتحدة النزاع حول أبيي بعثة يونيسفا سوق النعام مقالات ذات السوداني، فيتو - لبنى سعد شارك طباعة 18 حجم الخط سعر الجنيه السوداني ، شهد سعر صرف الدولار الأمريكي استقرارا أمام الجنيه السوداني في البنوك السودانية، مساء اليوم السبت 24 -10-2026. وترصد “فيتو” في السطور التالية آخر حركة لسعر الجنيه السوداني، مقابل الدولار في بنك السودان المركزي . سعر الجنيه السوداني مقابل الدولار في بنك السودان المركزي سعر الشراء: 4200 جنيه سوداني. سعر البيع: 3700 جنيه سوداني. الجنيه السوداني، تاريخ وتحديات العملة الجنيه السوداني هو العملة الرسمية لجمهورية السودان، ويرمز له بالرمز SDG، ويصدره بنك السودان المركزي، ويُستخدم في كافة المعاملات داخل البلاد. وشهد الجنيه السوداني عدة تحولات تاريخية منذ اعتماده، خاصة مع التغيرات الاقتصادية والسياسية التي مرت بها البلاد، بما في ذلك فترات التضخم المرتفع وإعادة هيكلة العملة؛ ما أثر في قيمته أمام العملات الأجنبية، وعلى رأسها الدولار الأمريكي. الفئات الورقية والمعدنية للعملة السودانية الفئات الورقية: -1 جنيه -2 جنيه -5 جنيهات -10 جنيهات -20 جنيهًا -50 جنيهًا -100 جنيه -200 جنيه -500 جنيه العملات المعدنية: -1 جنيه -50 قرشًا المرتبطة بالعمل العام كافيين لضمان الاستقرار المعيشي. أدى نزوح الملايين وتعطل المؤسسات الرسمية وتأخر صرف الرواتب إلى دفع الغالبية للبحث عن بدائل توفر مرونة أكبر وقدرة على التكيف مع الظروف المتغيرة. أفادت مصادر متخصصة في علم الاجتماع الاقتصادي بأن الوظيفة الحكومية كانت تمثل في السابق أداة للتخطيط الاجتماعي والمستقبلي للأسر السودانية، حتى مع محدودية الدخل. إلا أن الأزمة الحالية فرضت واقعاً جديداً جعل من تعدد مصادر الدخل استراتيجية ضرورية للبقاء، بدلاً من الاعتماد الكلي على جهة تشغيل واحدة قد تتوقف في أي لحظة. يرى باحثون أن انتشار العمل الحر والمشاريع الصغيرة لا يعني بالضرورة فقدان التقدير للعمل المؤسسي، بل يعكس تحول الوظيفة إلى مجرد أداة ضمن مجموعة أدوات لتأمين المستقبل. الحرب أثرت بشكل مباشر على الارتباط المكاني بالوظيفة، حيث بات النازحون مضطرين للبحث عن مصادر دخل تتناسب مع مواقعهم الجديدة بعيداً عن مقار عملهم الأصلية. تشير المصادر إلى أن الأجيال الشابة هي الأكثر استعداداً لتبني نماذج عمل غير تقليدية، نظراً لدخولها سوق العمل في بيئة اقتصادية مضطربة أصلاً. هذا الجيل بات يرى في whatsapp-stroke copylink جانب من اجتماع الرباعية الدولية بشأن السودان في جنيف (حساب مسعد بولس على إكس) Published On 24/10/2026 24/10/2026 عقدت مجموعة الرباعية الدولية بشأن السودان ، أمس الجمعة، اجتماعات في مدينة جنيف السويسرية، بحثت خلالها سبل مواصلة العمل المشترك لإنهاء الحرب في السودان ، مؤكدة أنه لا حل عسكريا للنزاع. وقال كبير مستشاري الرئيس الأمريكي دونالد ترمب للشؤون العربية والأفريقية، مسعد بولس ، إن الرباعية، التي تضم مصر والسعودية والإمارات والولايات المتحدة، اتفقت على أنه "لا حل عسكريا للنزاع في السودان". قصص مقترحة list of 2 items list 1 of 2 تأهل الزمالك والترجي ونهضة بركان لدور المجموعات بدوري أبطال أفريقيا والمريخ يودّع البطولة list 2 of 2 انشقاق 7 ضباط من الدعم السريع وانضمامهم إلى الجيش السوداني end of list وأضاف بولس أن المجموعة اتفقت أيضا على ضرورة توظيف قنوات الاتصال والأدوات والنفوذ المتاحة لأعضائها، مجتمعين وفرادى، للتواصل مع الأطراف السودانية المتحاربة والجهات الفاعلة الأخرى، بهدف إنهاء القتال عبر التفاوض. وأوضح أن هذه الجهود ينبغي أن تتكامل مع حوار سياسي شامل بقيادة سودانية، يفضي إلى الانتقال نحو الحكم المدني. وأشار بولس إلى أن اجتماعات الرباعية تناولت أيضا دعم جهود الآلية الخماسية الدولية لتيسير حوار سوداني شامل. تنسيق دولي لإنهاء الحرب وفي السياق، أفاد بولس بعقد اجتماعين مشتركين لأعضاء الرباعية والخماسية، بالتعاون مع شركاء دوليين وإقليميين، على هامش الاجتماع التشاوري السادس بشأن تعزيز تنسيق مبادرات وجهود السلام في السودان. وأضاف أن الاجتماعين بحثا خطوات محددة لتعزيز التنسيق بين المبادرات الدولية الرامية إلى إنهاء الحرب، وتسهيل حوار سياسي شامل يتيح التوصل إلى سلام دائم وانتقال حقيقي إلى حكومة مدنية. كما تناولت المناقشات، وفق بولس، سبل ضمان وصول المساعدات الإنسانية إلى المحتاجين وتعزيز حماية المدنيين والتخطيط لإعادة التأهيل والتنمية في السودان. وبحث المشاركون أيضا آليات التعاون بين الرباعية والخماسية وشركائهما الدوليين لدعم هذه الجهود. وكان مقر الأمم المتحدة في جنيف قد استضاف، الأربعاء الماضي، الاجتماع التشاوري السادس بشأن تعزيز تنسيق مبادرات وجهود السلام في السودان، بمشاركة ممثلين رفيعي المستوى من دول ومنظمات دولية وإقليمية. إعلان ويشكل الاجتماع آلية لتنسيق الجهود الدولية والإقليمية الرامية إلى إنهاء النزاع في السودان، دون مشاركة الحكومة السودانية أو قوات الدعم السريع في مداولاته. وتضم الآلية الخماسية الأمم المتحدة والاتحاد الأفريقي والاتحاد الأوروبي وجامعة الدول العربية والهيئة الحكومية الدولية المعنية بالتنمية في شرق أفريقيا ( إيغاد ). وفي سبتمبر/أيلول من العام الماضي، طرحت الرباعية الدولية خطة تدعو إلى هدنة إنسانية مدة 3 أشهر، تمهيدا لوقف دائم للحرب، تعقبها عملية انتقالية شاملة خلال 9 أشهر تقود إلى حكومة مدنية مستقلة. ومنذ أبريل/نيسان 2023، يخوض الجيش السوداني والدعم السريع حربا أسفرت عن مقتل Read Mastercard deploys AI, Tokenization to strengthen digital payment security By our staff reporter October 25, 2026 Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp Global payments technology company Mastercard is deploying artificial intelligence (AI) and tokenization technologies to strengthen security across Ethiopia’s rapidly expanding digital financial ecosystem. As Ethiopia expands digital payments beyond cash-based transactions to include virtual cards, mobile wallets and contactless point-of-sale systems, rising transaction volumes are increasing the need for stronger cybersecurity safeguards. Addressing these vulnerabilities is seen as essential to ensuring that efforts to expand financial inclusion remain resilient against increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. Ethiopia’s digital payment transformation is taking place alongside broader policy and regulatory reforms. The government has pursued measures to reduce reliance on cash and improve interoperability among banks, fintech companies and mobile money operators. However, security concerns have intensified alongside the sector’s growth. The National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE) reported that fraud losses reached 1.3 billion birr in 2024, while attempted cyberattacks targeting government and private organisations increased by 115 per cent in the first half of that year compared with the same period in 2023. Speaking to Capital , Shabir Ahmed, Mastercard’s Senior Vice President and Customer Solutions Center Lead for Africa, said secure payment platforms are essential to sustaining digital adoption in emerging markets. “Every single payment requires absolute trust,” Ahmed said. “At Mastercard, we have made substantial investments in our cyber and fraud mitigation capabilities globally. Today, we harness real-time artificial intelligence to evaluate transactions instantaneously.” He said the company’s systems assess risk factors within milliseconds to determine whether a transaction is legitimate or fraudulent, protecting consumers while enabling seamless commerce. Mastercard’s AI capabilities have continued to evolve. In March 2026, the company unveiled a transaction-specific foundation model, a large tabular model trained on hundreds of millions of anonymised transactions. The model is designed to identify fraudulent activity more accurately than traditional machine-learning systems by detecting complex relationships across large datasets that human analysts might overlook. It also aims to reduce false positives, which can result in legitimate transactions, including high-value purchases, being incorrectly flagged as suspicious. The technology marks a shift from conventional approaches that rely heavily on manually engineered features towards more advanced pattern recognition, helping payment providers respond to increasingly sophisticated fraud schemes. Beyond AI-powered risk assessment, Mastercard is advancing tokenization technology to protect sensitive payment information. Tokenization replaces a cardholder’s actual 16-digit Primary Account Number (PAN) with a digitally generated token that can be used for transactions without exposing the underlying card details. These tokens allow payment credentials to be stored and used across mobile devices, merchant systems and e-commerce platforms while reducing exposure of sensitive account information. If a merchant’s database is compromised, tokenized payment data can provide an additional layer of protection because tokens are generally restricted to specific devices, merchants or transaction contexts. This can reduce the risk of card-not-present fraud and the misuse of stolen payment credentials, although the level of protection depends on how the tokenization system is implemented. The benefits of tokenization have been documented in international markets. Industry discussions citing Visa data indicate that tokenized transactions can reduce e-commerce fraud rates compared with transactions using conventional card numbers. For Ethiopia, where digital payment adoption is expanding alongside concerns about fraud and consumer confidence, stronger payment security could play an important role in encouraging wider use of electronic transactions. The technology also supports Mastercard’s local partnerships, including its collaboration with Dashen Bank and Ethiopian Airlines. Recent co-branded offerings, including ShebaMiles Premium Cards, combine travel-related rewards with international payment capabilities across more than 200 countries and territories. As cross-border payments and digital services become more accessible, ensuring that transactions remain secure will become increasingly important for banks, merchants and payment service providers. Tokenization also underpins several consumer-facing payment services. It enables secure tap-to-pay transactions, supports digital wallets such as Google Pay where the service is available, and helps protect credentials used for recurring payments and international subscriptions. “When I travel today, I no longer rely on a physical card; wherever a contactless point-of-sale terminal is available, I simply tap my mobile phone,” Ahmed told Capital . “Through tokenization, you do not expose the physical card number—you use a secure tokenized identifier. Published 3 hours ago on October 24, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed addresses the 12th Tana High-Level Forum in Bahir Dar on October 24, 2026, discussing Ethiopia's sea access, political dialogue and economic sovereignty. Photo Credit: EBC / YouTube, Screenshot by Kulu Media Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has described reliable access to the sea as an existential issue for his country, while reaffirming his government’s willingness to pursue dialogue over political and security disputes. Addressing the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa in Bahir Dar, Abiy said Ethiopia’s population of more than 130 million made dependable international trade routes essential to its long-term economic development and national security. “For a nation of more than 130 million people, access to the sea is existential,” he told African leaders and delegates attending the forum. Abiy emphasized that Ethiopia would continue seeking solutions through dialogue and mutual benefit, framing maritime access as part of a broader strategy linking economic sovereignty, regional integration and lasting peace. His remarks came amid heightened tensions in the Horn of Africa, where Ethiopia’s pursuit of greater maritime access has become an increasingly sensitive diplomatic and security issue. Abiy Reaffirms Dialogue Amid Security Challenges The prime minister acknowledged the human consequences of conflict in Ethiopia, saying the effects of violence often extend far beyond the battlefield and continue to affect families long after fighting ends. He said protecting civilians and upholding the constitutional order remained central responsibilities of the government. At the same time, Abiy reiterated his willingness to engage groups prepared to abandon violence and pursue peaceful political dialogue. “We are ready and we will receive them with open arm and open heart,” he said. The remarks come as the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) and its Tigray Peace Force (TPF) allies continue military operations against TPLF-aligned forces in northern Ethiopia. Federal forces entered Mekelle earlier this month, and the TPLF subsequently confirmed its withdrawal from the regional capital. Abiy did not name the TPLF or specify particular armed organizations when extending his invitation to dialogue. The prime minister also discussed Ethiopia’s national dialogue process, saying recommendations had been submitted to parliament and regional governments. He called for those recommendations to be translated into concrete government decisions and practical measures. Reflecting on African-led mediation, Abiy argued that signing a peace agreement was only the beginning of a longer process requiring implementation, functioning institutions and improved livelihoods. His remarks come as the African Union continues efforts to preserve the peace process in northern Ethiopia, including a recent mediation initiative involving former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo. Ethiopia’s Sea Access and Regional Trade Abiy placed particular emphasis on Ethiopia’s landlocked position, arguing that dependence on routes through neighboring countries created long-term economic and security vulnerabilities. He said Ethiopia would continue pursuing dependable access through negotiations and arrangements intended to benefit all parties. “This concerns our security, our sovereignty and the future of our children,” he said. The prime minister linked Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions to the development of regional transport corridors and implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area. He argued that efficient cross-border transport could expand market access, support small businesses and reduce opportunities for illicit trade networks. His comments follow renewed regional debate over Red Sea security and maritime access. During a related discussion at the Tana Forum, Ethiopian National Security Adviser Redwan Hussein called for collective Red Sea security , emphasizing cooperation among coastal and landlocked countries. Abiy did not announce a new maritime agreement or identify a specific port arrangement in his speech. Energy Exports and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam Turning to economic development, Abiy presented the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam as an example of Ethiopia’s efforts to strengthen domestic infrastructure and expand regional economic cooperation. He said the country’s investment in the dam should translate into more reliable electricity, industrial development and improved livelihoods. According to the prime minister, Ethiopian electricity is reaching Kenya, Sudan, Djibouti and Tanzania. He portrayed cross-border energy cooperation as a practical example of regional integration, arguing that shared infrastructure could strengthen economic ties and reduce tensions. The speech did not provide separate figures for electricity exports to each destination. Gold Revenue and Domestic Mineral Processing Abiy also highlighted Ethiopia’s mining industry, saying gold generated approximately $5.6 billion in revenue during the country’s last fiscal year. The figure was presented by the prime minister and was not independently verified in the speech. He said Ethiopia had historically exported much of its gold in raw form but was now seeking to capture more value through domestic processing. Abiy pointed to the opening of a precious metals refinery in Addis Ababa, which he said could serve Ethiopia and neighboring African countries by refining and certifying gold. He argued that African countries should expand mineral processing, technical training and transport infrastructure to create jobs and retain more revenue from their natural resources. The prime minister also called for greater participation by African businesses in investment projects across the continent. Digital Ethiopia 2030 and Artificial Intelligence Technology was another central theme of the address. Abiy said economic sovereignty increasingly depended on countries controlling their own digital infrastructure, data systems and technological standards. He highlighted Ethiopia’s Digital Ethiopia 2030 strategy, including efforts to connect the Fayda digital identification system with payment platforms and public-service data exchange. The prime minister said such systems could improve access to government services while emphasizing the importance of protecting personal information and providing mechanisms for correcting errors. He also announced plans to develop an artificial intelligence university intended to welcome students from across Africa. According to Abiy, the institution would focus on developing technologies capable of addressing practical challenges. The speech did not provide an opening date or detailed funding arrangements for the proposed university. Ethiopia Prepares to Host COP32 Abiy also connected environmental protection and climate adaptation to Africa’s long-term security. He warned that drought and environmental degradation could intensify competition over land and water, potentially contributing to conflict. The prime minister said Ethiopia had planted more than 56 billion seedlings over eight years through its Green Legacy Initiative. He presented the program as part of efforts to protect agricultural land, water resources and rural livelihoods. Abiy also reaffirmed that Ethiopia would host the COP32 United Nations climate conference in 2027. He invited African governments to coordinate their positions ahead of the gathering, particularly on climate adaptation financing and investment in clean energy. The prime minister said African countries should prioritize financing that reaches farmers and pastoralists while supporting energy projects that create jobs. Calls for Stronger African Institutions Abiy concluded by calling for stronger African institutions with adequate financing, professional staffing and broader representation. He questioned whether the African Union’s current staffing adequately reflected the continent’s diversity and argued that regional organizations needed resources and authority appropriate to their responsibilities. He said African governments should contribute more consistently to institutions responsible for addressing shared security and development challenges. Referring to Ethiopia’s traditional practice of elder-led mediation, known as shimglina , Abiy emphasized the importance of trust, reconciliation and keeping commitments. His address placed economic resilience, political dialogue and regional cooperation at the center of Ethiopia’s stated approach to peace and security. The speech also underscored the government’s position that access to the sea remains a strategic national priority, even as Addis Ababa continues to advocate negotiated solutions. The 12th Tana High-Level Forum has also featured calls for stronger African economic independence and regional security cooperation. Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama urged African governments to strengthen economic sovereignty , expand domestic industries and finance their own peace operations. In a related Bahir Dar security dialogue, Ethiopian National Security Adviser Redwan Hussein called for collective Red Sea security , arguing that landlocked countries should also have a role in protecting regional maritime trade routes. Photo: Kenya Red Cross Society More than 14,000 Ethiopians have fled deadly fighting in the southern border town of Moyale into neighboring Kenya, as humanitarian agencies warn that shortages of food, clean water and sanitation facilities are threatening thousands of displaced families. The latest figures, reported on Saturday, October 24, 2026, mark a sharp escalation in the Moyale fighting displacement crisis, which began on October 21 amid tensions involving communities from Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional states. According to Anadolu Agency , Kenya Red Cross officials said more than 10,900 displaced people were sheltering in six temporary camps in the Kenyan border town of Moyale, while approximately 4,000 others were staying with relatives and host families. The reported numbers represent a substantial increase from the 2,500 displaced Ethiopians documented in earlier reports on October 23. The growing number of arrivals has intensified pressure on humanitarian services in the Kenyan border region, where emergency responders are struggling to meet the needs of families fleeing the violence. Kenya Red Cross Warns of Critical Shortages The Kenya Red Cross has appealed for additional humanitarian assistance as displaced families face increasingly difficult living conditions. Malik Adan, the organization’s head of the Upper Eastern region, told reporters that emergency shelters urgently needed more food, drinking water, sanitation supplies and toilet facilities. Humanitarian officials warned that inadequate sanitation could increase the risk of diarrheal diseases, particularly in crowded temporary camps where access to clean water and hygiene facilities is limited. The Kenya Red Cross has distributed tents, blankets, sleeping mats and other essential supplies while providing nutritional assistance to children and breastfeeding mothers. Local authorities have also pledged additional food supplies, including rice and beans, but relief workers remain concerned that available resources may be insufficient for the growing displaced population. The latest displacement figures underscore the rapid deterioration of humanitarian conditions since fighting erupted earlier in the week. When the violence first intensified, Kenyan authorities reported that hundreds of Ethiopians had crossed the border, many seeking temporary shelter with relatives and local residents. The movement has since expanded into a much larger humanitarian emergency. Death Toll Feared to Rise as Fighting Continues The humanitarian crisis follows several days of deadly clashes on the Ethiopian side of Moyale. At least nine deaths were reported on October 23, according to hospital information cited in earlier reporting. Humanitarian officials now fear that the overall death toll may have exceeded a dozen, although an updated casualty figure has not been independently confirmed. Residents have reported continued gunfire and shelling in affected areas, raising concerns about further casualties and displacement. The fighting has been linked to tensions between Oromo and Somali communities in southern Ethiopia. According to Anadolu Agency, a dispute involving the display of the Somali Regional State flag in an area administered by Oromia contributed to the latest confrontation. However, the precise sequence of events that triggered the violence, the identities of all armed participants and responsibility for individual attacks remain incompletely verified. The fighting has also affected civilians on the Kenyan side of the border. Earlier reports documented a woman injured by a stray bullet in Kenyan Moyale, demonstrating how violence close to the international boundary can threaten communities in both countries. Cross-Border Trade and Local Communities Under Pressure Moyale is one of the most important border crossings connecting Ethiopia and Kenya. The town serves as a commercial and transportation link between the two countries, supporting cross-border trade and economic activity. Continued insecurity threatens to disrupt business operations, transportation and the movement of goods, potentially affecting communities whose livelihoods depend on the border economy. The arrival of thousands of displaced Ethiopians has also placed additional pressure on Kenyan host communities. While temporary camps accommodate most of those reported to have crossed the border, thousands are staying with relatives and local families. Such arrangements can provide immediate protection but may become increasingly difficult to sustain if the fighting continues and displaced families are unable to return home. The crisis has also created additional demands on local healthcare facilities, water supplies and emergency services. Humanitarian Response Faces Growing Challenges The rapid rise in displacement highlights the difficulty of responding to sudden population movements in areas where humanitarian resources are already limited. The Kenya Red Cross and local authorities are coordinating relief efforts, but additional assistance may be needed if more civilians cross the border. The emergency is unfolding against a wider backdrop of humanitarian funding challenges in the Horn of Africa. Earlier this month, the United Nations refugee agency warned that funding shortages had disrupted protection services for refugees in Ethiopia, including the suspension of registration affecting tens of thousands of Eritrean and South Sudanese refugees. That separate crisis illustrates broader pressure on humanitarian operations across the region, although it is not directly connected to the Moyale fighting. For families fleeing Moyale, the immediate concerns remain personal safety, temporary shelter, clean water, food and access to medical care. The latest displacement figures suggest that the consequences of the fighting have extended well beyond the original areas of confrontation. With the security situation still uncertain, humanitarian organizations face the challenge of assisting thousands of displaced people while preparing for the possibility of further arrivals. Whether the situation stabilizes will depend partly on efforts to end the violence and restore security in the affected border communities. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Elevates Sea Access to Existential Security Issue Skip to content October, 2026 Birr Metrics News Feature Insights Interview Startups Editorial Digital Magazine Search for: Search Search Birr Metrics News Feature Insights Interview Startups Editorial Digital Magazine Ethiopia Elevates Sea Access to Existential Security Issue at Tana Forum Amanuel Kindeya October 24, 2026 Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed links Ethiopia’s dependence on foreign ports to national sovereignty, regional security and trade competitiveness as African leaders debate economic independence and geopolitical transformation. Ethiopia has renewed its diplomatic push for access to the sea, with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed (PhD) describing maritime access as an existential issue affecting the country’s long-term security, economic sovereignty and ability to participate in international trade. Addressing the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa in Bahir Dar on October 24, 2026, Abiy placed Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions within a wider continental discussion about economic independence, regional integration and Africa’s position in a changing geopolitical order. The Prime Minister said Ethiopia, a country of more than 130 million people, faces long-term strategic and economic constraints because its international trade routes pass through neighbouring countries. He maintained that Ethiopia would continue pursuing maritime access through dialogue and arrangements based on mutual benefit, presenting the issue as both a national security priority and an economic development concern. The remarks come as Ethiopia seeks to diversify its external trade routes, reduce dependence on the Djibouti corridor and negotiate more reliable access to international shipping networks. Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993, ending its direct access to the Red Sea through Assab and Massawa. The country subsequently developed a heavy dependence on Djibouti, which now handles more than 90 percent of its international merchandise trade. Djibouti’s port infrastructure, connected to Ethiopia by road and the Addis Ababa–Djibouti railway, serves as the country’s principal international trade gateway. The corridor supports imports of petroleum, machinery, industrial inputs and consumer goods, as well as exports of coffee, manufactured products and other commodities. This concentration means disruptions involving port operations, transport infrastructure, border procedures or regional security can affect Ethiopian importers, exporters and domestic supply chains. The financial implications extend beyond port charges. Importers and exporters incur costs associated with inland transportation, customs clearance, container handling, storage and cargo delivery between Djibouti and inland logistics facilities such as Modjo. The government has repeatedly identified high logistics costs and lengthy cargo-processing procedures as constraints on Ethiopia’s manufacturing competitiveness and export development. The maritime question has also become a major diplomatic issue in the Horn of Africa. In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with Somaliland concerning access to the coast. The agreement triggered opposition from Somalia, which considers Somaliland part of its sovereign territory, and led to a diplomatic dispute between Addis Ababa and Mogadishu. The two countries subsequently signed the Ankara Declaration on December 11, 2024, following mediation by Türkiye. Under the declaration, Ethiopia and Somalia reaffirmed respect for each other’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity while acknowledging the potential economic benefits of Ethiopia obtaining reliable access to the sea. The agreement envisaged mutually beneficial commercial arrangements, including contracts and leases, that would provide Ethiopia with secure and sustainable maritime access under Somalia’s sovereign authority. The declaration established a diplomatic framework for negotiations but did not itself grant Ethiopia a port or sovereign maritime territory. Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions also intersect with wider competition in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where strategic shipping routes connect the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal. Djibouti hosts foreign military facilities operated by several countries, including the United States, China, France and Japan. The wider maritime region has also faced security disruptions affecting international shipping, increasing attention to the reliability of trade routes. Against this background, Abiy linked Ethiopia’s position to the broader African challenge of securing predictable access to markets. He said transport corridors and more efficient cross-border arrangements were essential to enabling African producers to reach regional and international buyers. The issue is closely connected to the African Continental Free Trade Area, which aims to expand trade among African economies through tariff reductions, improved market access and measures addressing non-tariff barriers. For landlocked economies, implementing continental trade agreements also depends on transport infrastructure, customs cooperation and access to ports in neighbouring countries. The 12th Tana Forum, held from October 23 to 25 under the theme “Pathways to Peace in Africa: Economic Sovereignty and Geopolitical Transformation,” brings together African leaders, policymakers, researchers and representatives of regional institutions. Its agenda examines how control over economic resources, financial systems, trade networks and strategic infrastructure affects national sovereignty and the continent’s capacity to maintain peace. Abiy also presented Ethiopia’s domestic development and governance philosophy, Medemer, meaning synergy, as part of his wider argument for cooperation and collective African action. The Prime Minister has developed the concept through a series of publications addressing national unity, cooperation and economic transformation, and has increasingly connected it to regional and Pan-African priorities. The Tana Forum was established in 2012 by the Institute for Peace and Security Studies at Addis Ababa University, following the African Union’s 2009 Tripoli Declaration calling for African-led approaches to peace and security. It serves as an informal diplomatic and policy platform bringing together current and former African leaders, regional organisations, researchers and civil society representatives. The 2026 gathering is expected to involve around 250 participants and is examining economic sovereignty, resource governance, regional integration, institutional capacity and the effects of geopolitical competition on African security. Unlike formal African Union summits, the Tana Forum does not negotiate binding agreements. Its discussions are intended to inform policy debates and decision-making within African institutions. The Ethiopian government expressed concerns that the growing military presence in the region could destabilize the already fragile security situation. This warning comes as various nations vie for influence in the Horn of Africa, a strategically significant area that connects the Middle East and Africa. In an article published on Megatopia, Professor Al Mariam analyzed historical remarks made by Eritrean President Isaias Afewerki during a press conference in the early 1990s, noting that Egypt and Eritrea have historically coordinated to deprive Ethiopia of peace and generate continuous internal hardship. Al Mariam said the underlying strategic objective binding the axis is securing Egyptian dominance over the Nile waters. He explained that Egyptian political strategy relies on keeping upstream Nile Basin nations in a state of perpetual turmoil to restrict their ability to carry out vital riverine development projects along the Abay River. According to the analyst, President Isaias’ explicit acknowledgment of the campaign to "give Ethiopia work" reflects a deliberate strategy of exhaustion. By fomenting internal conflicts, funding armed insurgent groups, and conducting cross-border military incursions, the axis aims to force the Ethiopian government into continuous defense spending. This systematic diversion of national resources away from socio-economic and infrastructure projects serves to weaken state institutions and undermine national unity, the analyst elaborated. Al Mariam emphasized that the Eritrean regime effectively functions as a client state and proxy for Cairo, carrying out actions that compromise the stability of the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea corridor. He added that the calculated acts of destabilization orchestrated by Egypt and Eritrea constitute a grave threat not only to Ethiopia's sovereignty but also to the broader peace and security of the entire region. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Alimov told Russia’s Izvestia newspaper that Moscow is “ready to provide a platform for organizing contacts between their representatives in order to find compromise solutions,” including at the third Russia-Africa Summit scheduled for October 28-29 in Moscow. He expressed hope that both Ethiopia and Eritrea would take advantage of the opportunity. Alimov said the deterioration of relations between the two countries is a source of concern for Russia, which considers both nations long-standing and reliable partners. The Russian diplomat called on both sides to exercise restraint, strengthen confidence-building measures, and resolve their differences through dialogue and diplomacy. Eritrea Accuses Abiy of Pursuing War for Sea Access Eritrea’s Information Minister, Yemane Gebremeskel, has accused Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed of waging a war of aggression against Eritrea, arguing that Ethiopia’s pursuit of direct Red Sea access poses a threat to Eritrea’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Gebremeskel cited remarks Abiy made to parliament in October 2023, in which the Ethiopian leader stated his intention to secure “sovereign access to the sea, through negotiations if possible and by force if necessary.” Eritrea views this as a direct threat to its port of Assab and a pretext for territorial expansion. In a letter to the UN Security Council, Eritrea requested that the council “forcefully condemn Ethiopia’s deplorable declaration of war against Eritrea” and take “requisite deterrent measures” under Chapter VII of the UN Charter. Eritrea’s Foreign Minister, Osman Saleh, warned that the Ethiopian action would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilize the whole region.” Ethiopia responded with its own letter to the Security Council, invoking Article 51 of the UN Charter and accusing Eritrea of deploying infantry and mechanized units across the border and supporting, financing, arming, and directing insurgent groups. Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described Eritrea’s actions as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence.” Ethiopia’s Naval Expansion and the Red Sea Gambit The crisis is rooted in Ethiopia’s determination to re-establish a naval presence and secure direct access to the Red Sea, a goal that has intensified under Abiy’s government. Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea gained independence in 1993, and the country has repeatedly insisted that its “legitimate interests” in the Red Sea must be recognized. Ethiopia’s naval chief, Deputy Admiral Kindu Gezu, has acknowledged that the country’s naval force is being expanded from “zero,” with investments in training, infrastructure, and specialized combat units aimed at protecting national interests and responding to security challenges. The naval expansion comes as Ethiopia seeks to position itself as a maritime player in the Red Sea, despite not having a direct coastline. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Abiy’s Red Sea strategy , the Ethiopian Prime Minister has explicitly linked durable peace in the Horn of Africa to Ethiopia obtaining direct sea access, arguing that the absence of ports restricts the country’s economic expansion and international competitiveness. The Somaliland Option Despite its naval ambitions and its January 2024 memorandum of understanding with Somaliland that reportedly traded possible recognition for coastal access, Ethiopia has stopped short of formal recognition. The reason, according to Ethiopia’s Ambassador to Israel, Tesfaye Yetayeh Anteneh, is the risk of triggering a security collapse in Somalia. “The moment, for example, Ethiopia recognizes Somaliland, the Somali government will request Ethiopia to withdraw its troops from Somalia,” Anteneh said in an interview with i24NEWS. “And Al-Shabaab will get a free ride to attack both Somalia and Somaliland, even a spillover effect will come also to Ethiopia”. The ambassador described recognition as “a very delicate issue” and said Ethiopia “shouldn’t rush” into a decision that could unravel the security arrangement that keeps Ethiopian troops deployed in Somalia under the African Union mission. Ethiopia has been a central troop contributor in Somalia since 2006 and currently serves in the new African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), which began operating in January 2025. Anteneh’s explanation reveals a strategic calculation that treats recognition less as a question of principle than as a sequencing problem. Ethiopia wants sea access. It sees Somaliland as a potential pathway. But it also depends on cooperation with Mogadishu to maintain its military presence and combat Al-Shabaab. Recognition, at this juncture, would jeopardize that cooperation without guaranteeing the benefits. Somaliland’s ambassador to Israel, Mohamed Hagi, rejected this reasoning, arguing that recognition would strengthen Ethiopia’s security rather than undermine it, and that Mogadishu’s growing alignment with Ethiopia’s rivals posed a greater strategic threat. Somalia’s Parallel Fear: The Same Threat, A Different Border Eritrea’s alarm over Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions is not unique. Somalia shares the same fundamental fear, having already experienced what Eritrea now anticipates. In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Somaliland, the breakaway region Somalia considers its territory, granting Addis Ababa access to a 20-kilometer coastal strip at the port of Berbera for 50 years in exchange for potential recognition of Somaliland’s independence. Somalia rejected the agreement as a “blatant violation” of its sovereignty. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud described the deal as “nothing more than annexing part of Somalia to Ethiopia, and changing the borders of Somalia.” A Somali diplomat, speaking privately, put it more starkly: “This is not a port deal. This is a question of our existence as a nation.” As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Ethiopia’s Somaliland strategy , Addis Ababa has carefully positioned itself to move toward recognition without becoming diplomatically isolated. But the ambassador’s recent remarks suggest that the calculation is more complex than a simple trade of recognition for port access. The Ankara Declaration, brokered by Türkiye in December 2025, eased the immediate crisis by reaffirming both countries’ commitment to each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity while acknowledging Ethiopia’s interest in reliable sea access through commercial arrangements under Somali sovereignty. But the underlying tension remains unresolved. President Mohamud has said Somalia is open to Ethiopia using Somali ports, but only through direct negotiations with Mogadishu and under Somali sovereignty. For Somalia, the Eritrea-Ethiopia crisis is therefore not a distant dispute. It is a mirror image of its own confrontation with Addis Ababa, playing out on a different border. Eritrea’s accusation that Ethiopia is pursuing war to secure sea access echoes Mogadishu’s own experience with the Somaliland MoU . And Eritrea’s warning that Ethiopia’s actions could “destabilize the whole region” is a warning Somalia has already lived through. The Alamein Coalition and Its Fractures The Eritrea-Ethiopia standoff directly affects Somalia because both countries are signatories to the El Alamein Joint Declaration, signed on October 4, 2026, by Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea, and Somalia. That declaration formalized coordination on regional security, affirmed respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and stated that the management of the Red Sea is a responsibility exclusive to its littoral states. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the standoff , two of Somalia’s four partners in that declaration are now on the brink of war with each other, fracturing a coalition that was designed to present a united front against Ethiopian regional ambitions and Israeli recognition of Somaliland. The declaration explicitly rejected recognition of Somaliland and affirmed that Red Sea governance is the exclusive responsibility of littoral states, a provision clearly aimed at Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions. But with Eritrea and Ethiopia now exchanging accusations of aggression, the coalition’s ability to act collectively is severely compromised. Somalia’s Deputy Foreign Minister Hassan Mohamed Ali Nadar has said Mogadishu remains neutral in the Ethiopia-Eritrea dispute, maintaining relations with both countries and supporting peaceful solutions . That neutrality is pragmatic but precarious. Somalia has cultivated close relationships with both Egypt and Eritrea, viewing them as partners in its own domestic security appratus. But Somalia also relies on Ethiopia for security cooperation and troop contributions to the African Union mission. The prospect of an Ethiopia-Eritrea war places Mogadishu in an impossible position, forced to choose between regional partners whose conflict it cannot influence. Critical Note Russia’s offer to mediate is a diplomatic gesture that reflects Moscow’s desire to remain relevant in the Horn of Africa, where it has cultivated relationships with both Addis Ababa and Asmara. But mediation requires willing parties, and neither Ethiopia nor Eritrea has publicly accepted the offer or indicated readiness to compromise on the core issue: Ethiopia’s demand for Red Sea access and Eritrea’s determination to defend its sovereignty. The deeper problem is that the Eritrea-Ethiopia crisis is not a bilateral dispute that can be resolved through talks in Moscow. It is a structural collision between Ethiopia’s landlocked geography and its great-power ambitions, on one hand, and Eritrea’s insistence on the inviolability of its borders, on the other. Russia can provide a venue. It cannot provide a solution. For Somalia, the crisis is both a warning and a mirror. The Alamein Declaration was signed less than three weeks ago. Two (Eritrea an Sudan) of its signatories are now publicly throwing accusations. Somalia’s own confrontation with Ethiopia over the Somaliland MoU remains unresolved, and the same logic that drives Eritrea’s fears drives Mogadishu’s. Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access has already destabilized one border in the Horn. It now threatens to destabilize another. The Ethiopian ambassador’s explanation for why recognition is on hold is a reminder that Addis Ababa’s restraint is tactical, not principled. It depends on the costs of recognition remaining high. Somalia’s diplomatic strategy of aligning with Egypt and Eritrea against Ethiopian expansionism is understandable, but it depends on partners who are themselves locked in conflict. In the Horn of Africa, partnerships are provisional, and the only constant is the region’s capacity for sudden, destabilizing change. Share your story. Moscow's Deputy Foreign Minister, Alexander Alimov, expressed concern over the deteriorating relations and urged both nations to engage in dialogue. Eritrea's Information Minister accused Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed of waging a war for direct access to the Red Sea, which Eritrea views as a threat to its sovereignty. Eritrea has requested the UN Security Council to condemn Ethiopia's actions, while Ethiopia has countered with accusations of Eritrean aggression. The conflict is rooted in Ethiopia's desire to re-establish a naval presence after losing its coastline in 1993. Ethiopia's naval expansion aims to secure its interests in the Red Sea, which it links to economic growth. The situation also affects Somalia, which fears similar territorial threats from Ethiopia's ambitions, particularly regarding a recent agreement with Somaliland. The regional implications of this standoff remain significant, complicating diplomatic relations.

ethiopia.content: Kindiki arrives in Ethiopia for African security forum For You News Faida Cafe Shows Radio TV Podcasts Live Events Search Kindiki arrives in Ethiopia for African security forum By Citizen Reporter October 24, 2026 11:55 (EAT) Add as a Preferred Source on Google Follow us Follow on Whatsapp Follow on Google Follow on Twitter Kenya's Deputy President Kithure Kindiki is received by Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Satruday, October 24, 2026 for the 12th TANA High Level Forum on security in Africa, Bahir Dar, Ethiopia. /X/KITHURE KINDIKI Audio By Vocalize Deputy President Kithure Kindiki has arrived in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, to attend the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa. Kindiki was received at Bahir Dar International Airport on Saturday by Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. The forum, running from October 23 to 25, brings together African leaders, policymakers and other stakeholders to discuss the continent’s peace and security challenges under the theme, “Pathways to Peace in Africa: Economic Sovereignty and Geopolitical Transformation.” Discussions will examine how Africa’s management of its resources, economic institutions and regional integration can contribute to lasting peace. According to the organisers, the agenda includes resource wealth and monetary sovereignty for industrial development, macroeconomic governance, and the impact of illicit economies on regional stability. About 250 participants are expected, including sitting and former heads of state and government, diplomats, academics, civil society representatives and private sector leaders. Organised by the Institute for Peace and Security Studies at Addis Ababa University, the Tana Forum provides an informal platform for leaders and experts to debate African-led responses to security challenges. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia’s Strategic Interests, Historic Ties Bind It to Red Sea: Ambassador Zerihun - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia’s Strategic Interests, Historic Ties Bind It to Red Sea: Ambassador Zerihun - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia’s Strategic Interests, Historic Ties Bind It to Red Sea: Ambassador Zerihun 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, October 24, 2026 (ENA) —Ethiopia’s strategic importance, historical ties, and geographic realities make its connection to the Red Sea inseparable from its national interests, Director General for African Affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Zerihun Abebe said. Briefing journalists on the sidelines of the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa in Bahir Dar, Ambassador Zerihun underscored that Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access is rooted in history, geography, and national security. “We have repeatedly stated that the issue of a sea outlet is a matter of survival for Ethiopia,” he said, adding that the country has developed policy strategies to advance this objective. He stressed that Ethiopia cannot be excluded from discussions on the Red Sea, given its strategic position, security interests, and role in the wider region. The evolving regional realities, he added, call for cooperation that takes Ethiopia’s interests into account. Ambassador Zerihun reaffirmed Ethiopia’s commitment to working with regional countries to advance peace, development, and shared security, describing the Tana Forum as an important platform for strengthening cooperation and addressing common challenges. He also emphasized the need for a regional anchor capable of contributing to peace, development, and stability, asserting that Ethiopia has historically played—and continues to play—such a role. The remarks come as regional and international stakeholders gather in Bahir Dar for the Tana Forum’s Special Envoys’ Dialogue, which is examining the evolving geopolitics of the Horn of Africa and mounting security challenges in the Red Sea. In his welcoming remarks, National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS), Director General Redwan Hussein highlighted the strategic importance of the Red Sea and its maritime trade routes, warning that growing militarization, competition among external powers, and attacks on commercial shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait pose risks to regional stability. He emphasized that securing the Red Sea requires collective action by regional states and reliable international partners. He noted that Ethiopia has significant stake in maritime security as a country dependent on the Red Sea for its international trade. High-level discussions under the theme: “Regional Security in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea” brought together African and international envoys to examine the region’s changing security and geopolitical landscape. The 12th Tana High-Level Forum is being held under the theme “Pathways to Peace in Africa: Economic Sovereignty and Geopolitical Transformation,” bringing together policymakers, diplomats, and other stakeholders to explore African-led responses to the continent’s peace and security challenges. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

The Ethiopian government expressed apprehension that the heightened military presence in the region could destabilize maritime security and threaten trade routes vital for the economy. Ethiopia's concerns are compounded by the strategic importance of the Red Sea, which serves as a critical passage for global shipping. As foreign powers engage in military activities in the area, Ethiopia calls for dialogue and collaborative efforts to ensure peace and stability in the region. The situation remains precarious, with potential implications for both regional and international security dynamics.

President Donald Trump would like a few more Scandinavians to become Americans. The president vented during a Saturday rally in Perry, Georgia that he recently asked 10 Democratic Senators why the bulk of the USA's immigrants have to come from non-European countries. "I say, 'Why do we always have to take people from sh*thouse countries?'" Trump told the crowd. "Why can't we take people from like, well, Norway? Uhh, Sweden? Uhh, why not Denmark?" Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement That remark made a few people chuckle in the crowd, while one fella let out a loud "Yeah!" Trump then pivoted to championing Denmark for a moment, saying they "gave us Greenland." "You do know that? You don't read about it. We're working with them very closely," Trump said. As for the "sh*thouse" countries he was talking about, Trump said a prime example was Somalia. He said the East African nation is littered with scammers, so it makes no sense for the U.S. to bring them over. "You know, 98% of the people that we have here [from] Somalia don't work — they don't really have to work because they steal so much. They all have a Mercedes-Benz," Trump said. "Can you believe [it], low IQ and they live better than you do. Maybe they're not as low as we think." Advertisement Advertisement If this all sounds familiar, Trump said last December he would like to see the country allow in more Scandinavian immigrants . Around that same time, Trump said he did not want more Somalis like Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) moving to the States. "They contribute nothing. I don't want them in our country, I'll be honest with you," Trump said. "Some will say that is not 'politically correct.'" I don't care. Their country is no good for a reason." Shortly after he made the comment, federal prosecutors claimed a $9 billion "industrial-scale" fraud scheme was orchestrated in Minnesota, with the "vast majority" of culprits coming from Minnesota's Somali community. On Saturday evening, Trump mocked his longtime nemesis as her fraud probe heats up. Trump posted a meme with Omar's face on a iPhone screen that warned a "Scam Likely" call was coming in. According to a statement from the Ministry of Defence, the operation targeted militants who attempted to obstruct the advancing forces. Seven Al-Shabaab members were confirmed killed, while several others sustained injuries. The troops also seized various types of weapons that had been in the possession of the militants. The army is continuing operations to pursue fighters who fled the scene of the engagement. The Ministry of Defence commended the Danab Commandos for what it described as a “stern lesson” delivered to the Khawarij (Al-Shabaab), stating that the operation had commenced with a significant victory. The Danab Factor The Danab Brigade, an elite unit trained and equipped with U.S. support, has been at the forefront of Somali counterterrorism operations for years. The unit has conducted numerous raids and clearances against Al-Shabaab and ISIS-affiliated fighters, and AFRICOM commanders have described it as one of the most capable forces on the continent. In July 2026, the Danab Commandos conducted a similar operation in the Sablaale district of Lower Shabelle, killing seven militants including a senior commander and destroying two training facilities, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Sablaale operation . The unit has also targeted Al-Shabaab’s IED networks in the Harboole area of Lower Juba, dismantling cells responsible for planting explosives along civilian roads, as detailed in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Harboole operation . The Bay region has been a persistent front in the campaign against Al-Shabaab, with the militants maintaining a presence in rural areas and conducting periodic attacks on towns and military positions. Leego, located approximately 100 kilometers southwest of Mogadishu, has seen repeated clashes over the years. A Pattern of Sustained Operations Operation Banooda is the latest in a series of offensive operations announced by the federal government and its regional partners. The South West State has been a focal point of both military action and political tension, with the administration of President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed (Laftagareen) asserting that it is fully committed to supporting the national army’s efforts against Al-Shabaab, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the state’s position . The offensive comes amid a broader escalation of military activity across the country. In early October, Somali forces, local fighters, and the Xarardheere district administration conducted a planned operation against Al-Shabaab in two villages under the Caad area, securing the locations after targeting militant hideouts, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Xarardheere operation . In Hiiraan, the Somali National Army launched a series of operations against Al-Shabaab in areas under Maxaas district, targeting militant positions and movements in rural areas to weaken the group’s operational capacity, as detailed in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Maxaas operations . The operations followed the group’s capture of the strategic town in July 2025, a loss that exposed the federal government’s failure to support local Hawadle fighters who had borne the brunt of the fighting. The Danab Commandos have also conducted operations along the Jubba River in Jubaland, targeting Al-Shabaab positions, hideouts, and defensive fortifications in a coordinated air and ground assault that inflicted significant losses on the militant group, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Jubba River operation . The Broader Counterinsurgency Context The operation also unfolds against the backdrop of the ongoing AUSSOM transition, with the international mandate for the African Union mission set to expire at the end of 2026. The Somali government has been pressing its forces to take a greater lead in combat operations as international partners draw down their presence, as detailed in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the security transition . International support for these operations continues. U.S. Africa Command has conducted multiple airstrikes against Al-Shabaab targets in coordination with the Federal Government of Somalia, including strikes near Hargeisa Yare and the Dhobley airport in October 2026. Somali National Security Advisor Aweys Haji Yusuf Ahmed told the Global Security Forum in Doha that the country has liberated more than 55 percent of territory previously controlled by militant groups, freeing at least 1.5 million people. Critical Note The launch of Operation Banooda and the reported killing of seven militants is a tactical victory, and the Ministry of Defence is right to commend the Danab Commandos for their professionalism and effectiveness. The unit has consistently demonstrated its capability, and its role in this operation is a reminder of how central it has become to Somalia’s counterterrorism strategy. But tactical victories do not, by themselves, win insurgencies. Al-Shabaab has been pushed out of towns and districts before, only to regroup in rural areas and return when the army’s attention shifts elsewhere. The group’s capacity to conduct attacks in Mogadishu, and its ability to exploit political divisions between the federal government and regional states, remain significant. The political confrontation over the South West State, which has involved armed clashes between federal forces and Laftagareen-aligned militias, has complicated the counterterrorism effort and diverted resources from the fight against Al-Shabaab. The pattern of operations across the country, from Bay to Hiiraan to Jubaland, demonstrates that the SNA and its elite units are capable of conducting simultaneous and sustained offensives. But the government’s own claim that 55 percent of Al-Shabaab territory has been liberated is a measure of geographic control, not of durable security. The group’s ability to adapt, regroup, and exploit local grievances remains the central challenge. Operation Banooda will be measured not by the number of militants killed in its opening engagement, but by whether it can translate tactical gains into a durable security presence in the areas it clears. That requires not only military force but political stability, local governance, and the kind of intelligence cooperation that has often been undermined by the very political disputes the government is struggling to resolve. Privacy Policy Terms of Service Search GSEF 2026: Somalia's Ambassador to Kenya Says Somali Investors Are Tried and Tested October 24, 2026 5 min read HW By - Editor Hassan Wekesa Kenya, 24 October 2026 - Somalia’s Ambassador to Kenya, Jabril Ibrahim Abdulle, has hailed the Global Somali Entrepreneurship Forum (GSEF) as a platform that connects investors and businesses across the region, noting that trade improvements are evident. Speaking at the forum, now in its third year, he said remittances from the diaspora should go beyond consumption and be channelled into investment ventures back home, in the East Africa region and elsewhere where business environment is conducive. He noted that the forum continues to bring together investors, and that the eight member states of the East African Community (EAC) have a combined population of around 300 million people. The EAC member states are Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, South Sudan, and Somalia. “Trade improvements are evident,” Ambassador Abdulle said at the Radisson Blu Hotel, Upper Hill, Nairobi, adding that networks connect businesses. He urged the Somali diaspora to keep working hard and not to worry about how long they have stayed away from home. Abdelaziz Adan Abdullahi explains to attendees of the Global Somali Entrepreneurship Forum (GSEF) 2026 how BananaPay works. Photo: Dawan Africa To him, what counts is the remittances that enable those back home to invest in various ventures rather than simply consume. “A man is judged by what he or she brings home, not necessarily how long he or she has stayed away,” Ambassador Abdulle said. He said the forum comes hot on the heels of both Kenyan and Somali leaders attending the 25th Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe. He added that Kenya and Somalia share a lot in common, and that the relationship between the two neighbouring countries remains strong and warm. Ambassador Abdulle also said that envoys from many countries ask him how they can attract Somali investors, because “our people have been tried and tested.” Entrepreneurs Still Face Challenges Other speakers at GSEF 2026 said that while the Somali community is known to thrive in entrepreneurial ventures, both back home and in the diaspora, many businesses still encounter enormous challenges. Dr Ahmednur Abdi, the Chief Policy Advisor and former Permanent Secretary in the Office of the Prime Minister of the Federal Republic of Somalia, said entrepreneurs need simpler regulations and simpler dispute resolution mechanisms, among other interventions. He noted that, without any iota of doubt, the Somali people are resilient. “We should move from survival to reach potential. Somali innovation is visible,” he said. Dr Abdi urged both governments and investors to improve services and infrastructure. “We must ensure that the technologies we have help farmers, for instance, to reach markets,” he stated. Delegates follow proceedings during the Global Somali Entrepreneurship Forum (GSEF) 2026 at the Radisson Blu Hotel, Upper Hill, Nairobi, on Saturday, 24 October 2026. Photo: Dawan Africa He also called for collaboration between countries, their citizens and businesspeople so that they can tackle serious questions such as “can goods cross boundaries without delay?” Targeted investments in roads, energy and logistics, he said, would help streamline thriving business activity in the East African region. He urged governments in EAC member states to provide clear regulations. More from Kenya Somali President Meets Puntland Traditional Elder Amid Political Disputes. CS Aden Duale Jokes Somalia Has Many Gachaguas At GSEF 2026 Event in Nairobi However, Dr Abdi challenged the Federal Government of Somalia to wake up from its slumber, arguing that the private sector in Somalia was doing much better and that “the Government must keep at par with the private sector.” Dr Abdi is a seasoned governance and policy expert with more than 25 years of experience. He was glad to bring to the forum his deep expertise in public-sector reform, federalism, institutional development and lessons from post-conflict recovery. He established Somalia’s first Directors General Forum and has led the Federal Negotiation Technical Committee (FNTC), which brings together representatives of the Federal Government of Somalia (FGS) and the Federal Member States (FMS) to support negotiations on key federalism matters. He later led the State Formation Committee for the Northwest Somalia State. Duale: Somalia Must Find Political Goodwill The Chief Guest at the forum was Kenya’s Health Cabinet Secretary, Aden Duale, who said that people who do not know Somali business acumen and agility “take us for granted.” He said the time was ripe for Somalis back in the Federal Republic of Somalia to shape the destiny of their nation, because what is lacking there is political goodwill. “Countries that went under at the same time as Somalia are back on their feet. It is sad that 30 years later, Somalia still faces the same political fragility,” he said. He said many politicians in Somalia are his friends, but they must start thinking about how the country can turn around instead of burying their heads in the sand when it is supposed to sprout and grow. Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale addresses delegates as Chief Guest at the Global Somali Entrepreneurship Forum 2026 on Saturday, 24 October 2026. Photo: Dawan Africa He thanked the GSEF secretariat for offering the platform to investors, innovators and policymakers, among other stakeholders. He said that what counts now is for the platform to translate into practical opportunities, where entrepreneurs meet clients and strike meaningful business deals. “What matters now is not how many people attend this forum, but the business deals entrepreneurs get out of this distinguished gathering,” CS Duale stated. He said East Africa is at a critical moment, with countries still grappling with youth unemployment, poor infrastructure and other bottlenecks that bedevil the region. “The potential of our people can be tapped to realise full potential. We must create stronger pathways for entrepreneurs,” CS Duale said. He advised Somalia to follow in the footsteps of other EAC member states by ratifying all the requirements of the bloc, not just through the Legislative arm. He cited customs as an area the government should streamline if “Somalia wants to experience the business boom we see every day at the Kenya Ports Authority (KPA).” CS Duale said Kenya and Somalia have a strong connection, and that it is therefore important for both countries to enable entrepreneurs to access larger markets. “Government leadership is very important,” he advised. Businesses showcasing at the forum included Takaful Insurance, Beba Fleet, Fly Dubai, Amanah Insurance, BananaPay, Astral Aviation and Roasting Peacock. Abdelaziz Adan Abdullahi explains to attendees of the Global Somali Entrepreneurship Forum (GSEF) 2026 how BananaPay works. Photo: Dawan Africa Also present were Vickers Security Services Ltd, Aga Khan University, Aga Khan Hospital, Salaam Somali Bank, Travel Takaful, PayOn Time and Silva Gigiri. The two-day forum started on Saturday and ends on Sunday. Turyare, who currently serves as Somalia’s envoy to the Islamic Military Counter-Terrorism Coalition, cautioned that armed movements resembling those operating in Ethiopia’s Tigray, Amhara and Oromia regions could emerge in Somalia, particularly in Hiran, Middle Shabelle and Bay. He warned that the potential factions could eventually forge alliances with Al-Shabaab, the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group waging an insurgency against Somalia’s federal government, and urged authorities to prevent their emergence before they develop into a broader security threat. Turyare also issued a stark warning to those allegedly seeking to establish the armed factions, cautioning them against gambling with their lives by pursuing a course that could plunge the country into further violence. His remarks come amid growing reports in Somali local media suggesting that political disputes between Mogadishu and regional power brokers are increasingly intersecting with allegations of external military support and preparations for new armed formations. Sanbalolshe reportedly seeks military backing in Ethiopia At the centre of the latest concerns is former Somali intelligence chief Abdullahi Mohamed Ali Sanbalolshe, who, according to local media reports, is in the border town of Ferfer to receive military support from Ethiopia. The reports allege that Sanbalolshe intends to establish a powerful armed force capable of wresting control of the entire Hiran region from the federal government. His reported plans come against the backdrop of a growing political dispute involving his Hawadle clan and Mogadishu over the leadership of the Hirshabelle regional administration. The disagreement centres on the selection of the region’s president. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud backed Ali Gudlawe, who belongs to his own clan, for the position. Gudlawe was re-elected on Saturday, further intensifying the political tensions surrounding the regional leadership contest. The allegations concerning Sanbalolshe’s movements, military support and reported plans have not been independently verified. Middle Shabelle tensions and alleged UAE support A separate set of local media reports points to possible preparations for another armed faction in neighbouring Middle Shabelle. Abdullahi Mohamed Nur, a wealthy businessman affiliated with the clan of opposition leader Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, is reportedly planning to establish a guerrilla force in the region, allegedly with military support from the United Arab Emirates. The reports further claim that Nur possesses a substantial number of Ma’awisley fighters drawn from his own clan. Ma’awisley forces are locally organised armed groups that have played a significant role in Somalia’s fight against Al-Shabaab, particularly in central regions. Their potential mobilisation amid political disputes could add another layer of complexity to an already fragile security environment. The allegations of planned military assistance from the UAE, like those concerning Ethiopia, remain unverified. Bay remains a flashpoint after Laftagareen’s ouster The warnings come as Somalia’s federal government continues to grapple with guerrilla warfare by forces loyal to former Southwest State leader Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen. Laftagareen was ousted from power in March by a military operation, forcing his forces out of Baidoa, the interim regional capital. Since then, his fighters have shifted to guerrilla tactics, challenging federal authority across the region. According to the reports, Laftagareen’s forces made significant territorial gains last week, retaking five districts across Bay region, leaving Baidoa as the only town in the region outside their control. The renewed fighting underscores the difficulties facing the federal government as it attempts to consolidate its authority following the change of leadership in Southwest State. The developments also raise concerns that political confrontations, if increasingly pursued through armed proxies and irregular forces, could open additional fronts in a country already fighting a protracted insurgency. Fears of a wider security crisis The Somali federal government has not yet publicly commented on the reports concerning the alleged formation of new guerrilla factions, the purported external military backing or Turyare’s warning. The reports have nevertheless emerged amid mounting political tensions across Somalia, fuelling concerns that disputes between Mogadishu and its opponents could escalate into a wider cycle of armed confrontation. The potential consequences extend beyond individual regional power struggles. The emergence of additional armed factions in Hiran, Middle Shabelle and Bay could complicate counterterrorism operations, weaken federal authority and create opportunities for Al-Shabaab to exploit divisions among political and clan-based rivals. Turyare’s warning highlights the risk that armed groups established to advance political or regional interests could eventually become part of a more fragmented security landscape, particularly if they develop relationships with established militant organisations. For Somalia, the prospect of simultaneous conflicts involving federal forces, regional factions, clan-based militias and al-Shabaab presents a serious challenge at a time when the country continues to depend on extensive international political, financial and security support. Somalia has spent years rebuilding state institutions and security structures following decades of conflict and state collapse. A further spread of politically driven armed violence could undermine those gains, deepen regional instability and threaten the fragile process of state-building that has continued since 2004.
